note.p: 'Harriet Boinville (née Collins) had a long association with Godwin. In the 1780s her father became involved in Godwin’s and Marshall’s Marshall's ventures in the West Indies (see 1874 letters; and Shelley and His Circle, III: 255). As a child, Harriet lived on her father’s sugar estates in St. Kitts and St. Vincent, as well as in his London home. In 1793 she married Jean Baptiste Boinville, a Frenchman exiled in London who had served as the trusted aide to General Lafayette in the Paris National Guard. In 1813 he died during the retreat of Napoleon’s army from Moscow (see biography of Harriet Boinville).

Mrs. Boinville wore a red sash as a sign of her belief in republican ideals (Bieri, 259; Cameron, 244, 246). She often called herself a child of the revolution, according to her grandson Charles, who also noted her Godwinian enthusiasm for the New Philosophy of the Enlightenment, which he considered “the false philosophy of the age” (Constable, 11).

Harriet Boinville’s family and Godwin’s family were closely entwined. In 1812, Harriet’s daughter, Cornelia Boinville, married Thomas Turner, Godwin’s protégé. In 1818 Harriet’s son, Alfred Boinville, married Godwin’s friend Dr. William Lambe. Percy Bysshe Shelley and his wife, Harriet Shelley (née Westbrook) were briefly part of the Godwin-Boinville circle, which also included Cornelia Newton (née Collins) and John Frank Newton, as well as Thomas Jefferson Hogg and William Love Peacock. Harriet Boinville’s friendship with Mary Godwin and her sister Clara Mary Jane Clairmont (Claire) began in the early 1800s in William and Mary Jane Godwins’ home when they were girls (see Seymour, 65). This relationship ruptured in 1814 when the sisters ran off to Europe with Percy Bysshe Shelley. Mrs. Boinville sided with the Godwins and with the jilted Mrs. Shelley (see biography of Harriet Boinville, 107, 131).

After Harriet Boinville moved to Paris in the 1820s, her friendship with the Godwins’ two surviving daughters, Mary and Claire, resumed. She wrote to Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley (née Godwin) in 1829, 1836, 1837, and 1839 (see Abinger collection). The sisters’ letters to each other in the 1830s and 1840s describe in detail Mrs. Boinville and members of her family (see The Clairmont Correspondence). In Godwin’s diary Harriet Boinville is described as either Mrs Boinville or H Boinville. Miss Boinville or C Boinville is Cornelia Boinville. There are many references to ‘H and C Boinville’ calls, and Thomas Turner is closely linked, suggesting that Godwin may have been facilitating the courtship with Harriet’s daughter. “Two Boinvilles” refers to Harriet and her husband Jean Baptiste. On 27 April 1810 the diary refers to “Mrs. Boinville: 3 Boinvilles.” This has been taken to mean Harriet Boinville and her husband and their two children Cornelia and Alfred. Per usual practice, meals at ‘Boinville’s’ have been taken as including both husband and wife, although meals at ‘H Boinville’s’ include just Harriet.
